title: Buying Gold This Dhanteras? Six Details to Check on the Bill Before You Pay
excerpt: Dhanteras falls on Friday, November 6, and jewellers will be crowded. The hallmark, the HUID number, the day rate, making charges, stone weight and the GST line each need to be on the invoice — here is how to verify them in the shop, before money changes hands.
body:
• Dhanteras is Friday, November 6, the biggest gold-buying day of the year — and the checks that protect you take two minutes at the counter, before you pay, not after.
  • Do not pay for jewellery until you have seen the BIS hallmark and its 6-character HUID number; you can verify the HUID free in the BIS Care app and see the item hallmarking details.
  • The per-gram rate is only part of the bill: making charges and 3 per cent GST are added on top. On Rs 1,00,000 of gold with Rs 12,000 making charges, GST alone is Rs 3,360, for a total of Rs 1,15,360.
  • Keep the itemised invoice: weight, purity, HUID, rate, making charges and GST on separate lines. You will need it to sell, exchange or pledge the piece later.

Dhanteras, on Friday, November 6, opens the five-day Diwali festival, and buying gold or silver on the day is a tradition most families observe at some scale — a coin, a pair of earrings, a chain. It is also the most crowded, most hurried day of the jeweller year, which is exactly when bill errors and quiet overcharges slip through. Livemint set out six details to check in the bill before paying; here is each one, with how to verify it on the spot.

1 and 2: The hallmark, and the HUID behind it

Every hallmarked piece carries three marks: the BIS logo, a purity grade such as 22K916 (22-karat, 91.6 per cent pure), and a unique 6-character HUID — Hallmark Unique Identification — code. The HUID is the part most buyers skip, and it is the part that actually protects you: type it into the free BIS Care app and the item hallmarking details come up. If the code on the piece does not match the code printed on the bill, stop there.

3 and 4: The rate, and the making charges

The bill should show the day gold rate per gram for the purity you are buying, applied to the net weight. On top of that come making charges, which are the negotiable part of the purchase: they run from about 6 per cent to about 25 per cent of the gold value, with heavier designs costing more, according to Aditya Birla Capital buyer guide. For stone-studded pieces, insist the jeweller weighs the item in front of you and records both gross and net gold weight, with stone costs as their own line — you should not pay gold rates, or gold making charges, on the weight of stones, Angel One advises.

5 and 6: The GST line, and the buyback terms

GST on gold jewellery is 3 per cent of the total amount including making charges. The arithmetic is worth doing once, slowly, because it is the line buyers most often wave through: gold worth Rs 1,00,000 with Rs 12,000 of making charges attracts Rs 3,360 of GST, taking the bill to Rs 1,15,360, in the worked example in Aditya Birla Capital guide. Finally, get the buyback and exchange terms in writing before you pay — making charges and GST are generally not recovered when you sell, so the terms you are offered today are the real resale terms. Coins and bars carry the same 3 per cent GST; many banks that sell coins do not buy them back, so ask before choosing a bank counter over a jeweller.

None of this requires expertise, only sequence: hallmark, HUID, rate, making charges, weight, tax. Run the checks in that order and a Dhanteras purchase stays what it is meant to be — a festive one.
